builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
summary: LED replaces replacement-only token editing in diffusion language model decoding with Levenshtein-style insertion, deletion, and replacement, trained via on-the-fly LCS-based edit supervision and multi-stage fine-tuning rather than annotated labels. The cost is a post-training pipeline on a 16B-parameter model, including multi-stage training where each stage's output feeds the next, which is impractical on a single 24 GB GPU and adds modest per-forward decoding overhead (6.14 to 7.05 tokens per forward). It can fail if applied to models whose base decoding already saturates, if the reconstructed edit supervision misaligns with true error modes, or if confidence-guided decoding is already available, since the largest gains appear in the confidence-free setting.
rationale: The gains are real but require supervised fine-tuning of a 16B diffusion model with multi-stage training, which exceeds a single 24 GB GPU and a limited cloud budget, so the reader should track the method rather than adopt it now.
technique: Levenshtein insertion/deletion editing for diffusion LM decoding

claims.statement: LED replaces replacement-only token editing in diffusion language model decoding with Levenshtein-style insertion, deletion, and replacement, trained via on-the-fly LCS-based edit supervision and multi-stage fine-tuning rather than annotated labels. The cost is a post-training pipeline on a 16B-parameter model, including multi-stage training where each stage's output feeds the next, which is impractical on a single 24 GB GPU and adds modest per-forward decoding overhead (6.14 to 7.05 tokens per forward). It can fail if applied to models whose base decoding already saturates, if the reconstructed edit supervision misaligns with true error modes, or if confidence-guided decoding is already available, since the largest gains appear in the confidence-free setting.

On LLaDA2.1-Mini 16B, LED raises the twelve-benchmark average from 54.86 to 57.10 (+2.24 points) under confidence-guided decoding and from 27.52 to 47.19 (+19.67 points) under confidence-free decoding; at block size 128 the average rises from 36.97 to 51.34.
